key_findings: Achieved quantum supremacy using a programmable superconducting processor.

The Sycamore processor sampled a quantum circuit a million times in approximately 200 seconds, while a state-of-the-art classical supercomputer would take approximately 10,000 years for the equivalent task.
Demonstrated that quantum speedup is achievable in a real-world system and is not precluded by any hidden physical laws.
Quantum processors can now perform computations in a Hilbert space of dimension 2^53, beyond the reach of the fastest classical supercomputers.
The experiment marks the first computation that can be performed only on a quantum processor.
The fidelity of the quantum circuit is well predicted by a simple model in which the individually characterized fidelities of each gate are multiplied together, supporting a digitized error model.
High-fidelity single- and two-qubit gates were developed and executed simultaneously across a two-dimensional qubit array.
The experiment utilized 53 functioning qubits out of a total of 54 in the Sycamore processor.
The error rates for single-qubit gates were found to be approximately 0.15%, and for two-qubit gates, approximately 0.36% when isolated, and 0.62% during simultaneous operation.

The fidelity of the largest random quantum circuits with 53 qubits was predicted to be 0.2%, with experimental verification in the supremacy regime showing average fidelity greater than at least 0.1%.
